issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: Self-blame is difficult to justify clinically here because the profile contains no Negative Appraisal items and the formulation marks Negative Appraisals as inactive with no links to other active nodes. This item introduces a strong appraisal theme that is not supported elsewhere in the selected profile.

issues.item: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
issues.explanation: Avoiding driving or being a passenger in a vehicle is not well grounded by the rest of the profile. The memory and threat items center on sensory re-experiencing, confinement/safety, and startle, but nothing suggests a vehicle-related trauma cue. For terrorism this could occur, but in this profile it appears disconnected from the other selected items and from the inactive Triggers network.

issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: Self-blame is not well supported by the rest of the profile. There are no Negative Appraisal items and no other selected items suggesting guilt, responsibility, or moral injury; for a terrorism trauma this item can occur, but here it feels clinically disconnected from the rest of the presentation.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: Door/window checking is a poor fit with the rest of the threat profile and trauma context. The other threat items suggest generalized hypervigilance/startle and restricted safety, but no trigger, memory, or appraisal content links the terrorism trauma to home-intrusion fear or lock-checking specifically. This makes the item feel mismatched to the formulation and selected symptoms.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategy items are not well supported by the rest of the profile. The cognitive formulation only links Memory with Maladaptive Strategies, so strategies should plausibly arise from intrusive trauma memory content. However, the selected strategies are heterogeneous and weakly connected to the memory and threat items provided.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
issues.explanation: Self-blame introduces a strong negative-appraisal theme, but no Negative Appraisals items are endorsed and that node is structurally inactive in the formulation. This makes the self-blame item stand out as clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: Self-blame is not inherently impossible after terrorism, but in this profile there are no Negative Appraisals items at all and the formulation specifies Negative Appraisals as inactive with no links to other nodes. A prominent self-blame strategy therefore lacks support from the rest of the profile and does not fit the stated formulation well.

issues.item: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
issues.explanation: Avoiding driving or being a passenger in a vehicle is too specific without any corresponding trigger, memory content, or threat item tied to vehicles/transport. For a terrorism trauma this could occur, but here the rest of the profile centers on generalized hyperarousal and sensory memory rather than transport-related danger, making this item insufficiently supported and cross-node inconsistent.

issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: Self-blame is clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile. The other endorsed items center on sensory trauma memories and current threat/hypervigilance after terrorism, but there are no Negative Appraisal items supporting a guilt/responsibility theme, and the formulation leaves Negative Appraisals inactive. In this profile, repeated self-blame stands out as an isolated process that is not linked to the active Memory↔Threat pattern and is therefore clinically incoherent relative to the selected items and formulation.

issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies are not well anchored to the rest of the profile. The memory and threat items describe a classic sensory re-experiencing / hypervigilance pattern after terrorism, but self-blame, avoiding driving, and avoiding conflict introduce themes that are not represented in the memory or threat content and therefore do not cohere well with the active Memory↔Threat formulation.

issues.item: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
issues.explanation: Within Maladaptive Strategies, the selected items point in three quite different directions: moral/self-evaluative coping (self-blame), transport-specific avoidance (driving/passenger), and interpersonal avoidance (conflict). This breadth is not impossible, but here it lacks supporting trigger, appraisal, or memory content to connect them into one coherent terrorism-related syndrome.

vignette:
At 72, Minh had spent much of his life working with refugees, and he had built a reputation among colleagues as steady, patient, and hard to rattle. He was married, lived with his wife in a modest apartment, and still went into his office several days a week as a refugee aid worker, though the work no longer felt as familiar or manageable as it once had. His difficulties began after a terrorist attack that unfolded in the course of the very work that had given structure to his adult life. He had been traveling with a small team and several families he was helping to relocate when the attack erupted without warning. In his memory, the details do not arrive as a coherent story so much as a sequence of images: people ducking, bodies pressed low, a flash of movement, dust, shattered sound, and the look on frightened faces. When he tries to describe it, he often says it feels unreal, as if it must have happened to someone else, because it was too extreme to fit inside an ordinary life and too violent to seem believable even to him. Yet the pictures remain vivid. He sees the scene in fragments, and when he thinks back to it he sometimes hears the sounds again in his head, as if they are replaying just behind his ears-the sharp, jarring noises of the attack and the panic around him.

In the months that followed, Minh found himself repeatedly returning to the event in his mind, not in a way that felt voluntary or helpful, but as a stubborn accounting of what he believed he should have done differently. He blamed himself again and again for not preventing it, for not noticing something sooner, for not being more alert to danger. Even when others told him the attack had been sudden and no one could have controlled it, he kept circling back to his own part in it. The self-blame became part of his private conversations with himself, especially at night, when the day's distractions were gone and the images seemed closest. His wife noticed that he became quieter after dinner, staring into space for long stretches, then suddenly speaking with harsh certainty about his own failure. Minh did not frame it as guilt in any formal sense; to him it felt more like a moral accounting that never closed.

As time went on, he began narrowing his world. He no longer felt comfortable in vehicles, whether driving or riding as a passenger, and he arranged his life to avoid them whenever possible. What had once been a routine part of his work now felt intolerable, because being in a car placed him in a moving, enclosed space where he could not see enough, could not leave quickly, and could not trust what might happen around the next corner. He also became wary of any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation. In the office, where refugee cases often required difficult conversations and occasional disputes over paperwork, he would step back from meetings he once would have handled without hesitation. If a discussion grew tense, he found reasons to leave, saying he needed to make a call or check on a file. Over time, this changed how he worked. Colleagues began routing more contentious issues around him, and though he remained respected, he felt increasingly sidelined from the aspects of the job that had once given him a sense of usefulness.

Minh's sense of safety also became highly restricted. He said he only felt secure in a very small number of places, mainly at home and in one corner of his office where he could sit with his back to the wall and see the door. Even there, he remained watchful. Ordinary sounds made him jump-door slams, sudden voices in the hallway, a dropped object in the kitchen. He knew these noises would not bother most people, yet his body reacted before he could reason with himself. He found himself scanning streets, rooms, and entrances automatically, always alert for what might happen next. This hypervigilant watchfulness was exhausting, but he could not simply switch it off; it had become the way he moved through the world.

He and his wife now organize daily life around these limitations, and the consequences have become more visible over time. She does more of the shopping and most of the driving, while Minh avoids invitations that might place him in crowded or unpredictable settings. His world has become smaller and more rigid, and he has only recently admitted that he needs help because the strain is no longer something he can manage in silence. What brought him to treatment was not one dramatic breakdown but the accumulation of these changes: the shrinking places where he felt safe, the constant startle, the repeated self-accusation, and the way his work-once central to his identity-had become harder to do. Minh came hoping to understand why the memory still felt so immediate and strange, why his body stayed on guard, and whether he could recover some freedom without feeling as if he were betraying the people he had tried so hard to help.
